D001.title: Prohibition on coordinated pricing algorithms for residential rents and occupancy
D001.requirement: City of Berkeley landlords may not use a coordinated pricing algorithm when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley. It is also unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide such an algorithm to Berkeley landlords for setting or recommending rents or occupancy levels.
D001.key_value: Ban on sale or use of coordinated pricing algorithms using nonpublic competitor data less than 90 days old

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to City of Berkeley landlords and residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.
coverage.summary: The ordinance covers coordinated pricing algorithms used for residential dwelling units in Berkeley by Berkeley landlords, without stated unit-count, building-age, or owner-occupancy limits.

D001.exemptions: The definition excludes aggregated and anonymous reports that do not recommend future lease terms; products used to establish rent or income limits under affordable-housing guidelines; and information used for project-financing market research, appraisals, or software-development research, testing, or training, as specified.
D001.penalty: The City Attorney may seek damages, injunctive relief, restitution/return of illegal profits, civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, and attorney’s fees and costs. An aggrieved tenant may sue for subsection B violations for injunctive relief, money damages, civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, and attorney’s fees and costs.
D001.interaction: The ordinance states it does not regulate the amount of rent a landlord may charge and is not intended to prevent software that helps landlords manage units generally or uses public data.
D001.quoted_span:
Instead of waiting for court processes which may take years to resolve, this 
ordinance prohibits the sale or use of coordinated pricing algorithms for the purpose of 
setting rents on residential dwelling units in the city of Berkeley, to bring immediate relief 
to Berkeley tenants, as well as to put landlords on equal footing with their competitors.
D001.conflict_note: The document states the ordinance was “passed to print and ordered published” and refers to posting copies “prior to adoption,” but does not state final adoption or an effective date.

D002.key_value: Up to $1,000 per violation; each month of use for each affected dwelling unit may be a separate violation

D002.penalty: Civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; each month of use for each affected dwelling unit may constitute a separate violation.
D002.quoted_span: The ordinance prohibits landlords from using qualifying algorithmic devices that calculate nonpublic competitor information to advise on rent or occupancy. Each month of use for each affected dwelling unit may constitute a separate violation, and tenants may seek damages, injunctive relief, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.

D003.law_name: Ronald V. Dellums Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
D003.title: Berkeley fair-chance housing restrictions on criminal-history screening
D003.requirement: Berkeley rental housing providers may not ask about or use criminal history or criminal background checks in rental advertising, applications, tenant selection, or tenancy decisions. If a landlord takes action against an applicant or tenant based on criminal history, the landlord must provide written notice and an opportunity to respond.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Exemptions include lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back under BMC 13.76.130 A.9; and units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates.
coverage.summary: Applies to Berkeley rental housing providers with regard to current or prospective tenants, subject to listed exemptions.

D003.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; public housing/Section 8 properties limited exemptions; owner-occupied properties between 1-3 units in which an owner of record resides in one of the units as their primary residence; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back to their home in accordance with BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenant(s) seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates.
D003.penalty: Administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation, civil damages including actual damages or three times the amount of one month's rent, punitive damages, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief.
D003.interaction: The document states the ordinance has limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties and for owner move-back rental agreements under BMC 13.76.130 A.9.
D003.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.

D004.law_name: Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance
D004.effective_date_basis: At its October 16, 2025 Special Meeting, the Rent Board approved relocation assistance payment increases that will go into effect on January 1, 2026.
D004.title: 2026 owner move-in eviction relocation assistance adjustment
D004.requirement: For an owner move-in eviction, the owner must pay relocation assistance to the tenant. Beginning January 1, 2026, the standard payment is $19,413, with an additional $6,471 for qualifying households.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies in the event of an owner move-in eviction; qualifying-household criteria are not stated in the document.

D004.interaction: The document states that both the Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance and the Ellis Implementation Ordinance index relocation payments to inflation and require annual publication of increases.
D004.quoted_span: The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction.

D004.effective_date_basis: At its October 16, 2025 Special Meeting, the Rent Board approved relocation assistance payment increases that will go into effect on January 1, 2026.
D004.title: 2026 Ellis Act eviction relocation assistance adjustment
D004.requirement: For an Ellis Act eviction to remove a property from the rental housing market, the owner must pay the same relocation assistance amounts. Beginning January 1, 2026, the standard payment is $19,413, with an additional $6,471 for qualifying households.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to tenants evicted so the owner can remove a property from the rental housing market; qualifying-household criteria are not stated in the document.

D005.title: Tenant screening fee limits and required refunds/disclosures
D005.requirement: A landlord may charge a prospective tenant a screening fee only for permissible screening costs and may not charge it if no rental unit is actually available. The applicant should receive a credit-report copy within 7 days after the landlord receives it, a receipt and itemized accounting, and a refund of any unused portion; if the applicant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when a landlord charges a prospective tenant a screening fee to obtain information such as a consumer credit report; other statutory coverage details are not stated in the document.
coverage.summary: Prospective tenants applying for available rental units are covered when a landlord charges a tenant screening fee.

D005.exemptions: The landlord must return a screening fee to any applicant not selected, unless the landlord has a policy to review applications in the order received, rent to the first qualified applicant, and not charge a screening fee to any applicant not considered.
D005.interaction: The Berkeley page states that screening and application fee limits exist under both state and local law, and Berkeley requires owners to disclose the state fee cap and rights statement before taking a fee.
D005.quoted_span:
The maximum tenant screening fee for 2026 is
$68.96
Landlords may use screening fees to obtain information about a prospective tenant like a consumer credit report. Prospective tenants should expect to receive a copy of their credit report within 7 days of receipt by the landlord

D005.title: Berkeley tenant screening and application fee disclosures and limits
D005.requirement: When a Berkeley residential rental owner or agent charges a fee to buy a consumer credit report or process an application, the owner must give a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and state the maximum fee cap before receiving the fee. An owner or agent also may not charge an existing tenant a non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy or to add, replace, or remove a roommate in a pre-existing household.
D005.key_value: Disclosure of California Civil Code Section 1950.6(b) maximum fee cap; no non-refundable application-related fees for existing tenancies

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when an owner or agent receives a request to rent residential property in Berkeley and charges a consumer-credit-report or application-processing fee; also applies to existing tenants renewing or changing roommates.
coverage.summary: Berkeley residential rental applications involving screening/application fees, and existing Berkeley residential tenancies involving renewal or roommate-change fees, are covered.

D005.penalty: Chapter 13.78 applies regardless of contrary lease language, and any provision of an existing rental agreement or lease that violates the chapter is unenforceable.
D005.interaction: The Berkeley ordinance requires disclosure of rights and the maximum cap under California Civil Code Section 1950.6(b) and applies despite contrary language in rental agreements.
D005.quoted_span: An owner of residential rental property (or the owner’s agent) cannot charge a non-refundable fee to any existing tenant for the purpose of renewing a tenancy, in whole or in part, including any fee associated with the departure of a roommate or to request to add or replace a roommate in a pre-existing household.

D006.law_name: Measure BB amendments to Berkeley Rent Ordinance
D006.title: Measure BB rent-control and rent-increase changes
D006.requirement: For fully covered Berkeley rental units, annual rent increases remain tied to the Rent Ordinance CPI formula but the Annual General Adjustment cannot exceed 5%. Landlords of fully covered units may charge utilities only as part of base rent or through a separately metered utility account in the tenant’s name, and capital-improvement rent-increase petitions may be filed only for completed improvements.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Units where the tenant shares kitchen or bath facilities with the landlord are exempt only if the landlord lived in a unit on the same property at the start of the tenancy; subsidy-related coverage may depend on unit type and whether federal law, state law, or administrative regulation exempts the unit from rent control.
coverage.summary: Rent-control limits apply to fully covered units, described as most multifamily properties built before 1980, certain single-family home tenancies, certain room rentals, and some government-owned or subsidized units depending on legal restrictions.

D006.exemptions: Partially covered unit types include new construction units with a certificate of occupancy issued after 1980, most single-family homes, and most condominiums; certain subsidized units are only partially covered where federal law, state law, or administrative regulation prohibits rent control.
D006.interaction: The document states that federal law, state law, or administrative regulation may prohibit Berkeley rent control for certain subsidized units, making them partially rather than fully covered.
D006.quoted_span: The maximum AGA is 5%. This means that, if the formula in the Rent Ordinance results in an AGA that is greater than 5%, the AGA approved by the Board for that year can be no more than 5%.

D006.law_name: Measure BB amendments to Berkeley Rent Ordinance
D006.title: Measure BB just-cause eviction changes
D006.requirement: Tenants in fully or partially covered Berkeley units may be evicted only for just cause; Measure BB bars nonpayment eviction unless the rental debt is at least one month of the applicable HUD Fair Market Rent, bars eviction for refusing to sign a substantially similar fixed-term lease, and tightens material-lease-breach evictions. Termination notices must include Rent Board counseling information, and landlords must file copies of eviction notices and lawsuits with the Rent Board within three business days after service.
D006.key_value: Nonpayment eviction requires rental debt equal to or greater than one month of Fair Market Rent; eviction documents due to Rent Board within 3 business days

coverage.other_unresolvable: Coverage depends on whether the unit is fully or partially covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance; shared kitchen or bath units are exempt only if the landlord lived in a unit on the same property at the start of the tenancy, and subsidy-related coverage may depend on federal, state, or administrative rent-control restrictions.
coverage.summary: Just-cause eviction protections apply to tenants in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley’s Rent Ordinance.

D006.exemptions: Units exempt from the Berkeley Rent Ordinance are not described as covered by these just-cause protections; the document specifically notes a shared-kitchen-or-bath exemption only when the landlord lived on the same property at the start of the tenancy.
D006.interaction: The document describes the just-cause protections as part of Berkeley’s Rent Ordinance and notes that units may be fully covered, partially covered, or exempt under that ordinance.
D006.quoted_span: In Berkeley, tenants in units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance cannot be evicted unless there is "just cause” (previously called “good cause”). Measure BB has changed some just causes, eliminated one just cause, added new requirements for eviction notices

D007.effective_date_basis: Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may only charge one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units
D007.title: Statewide security deposit cap
D007.requirement: Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may charge no more than one month's rent as a security deposit for either unfurnished or furnished units. Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total may charge up to two months' rent if ownership is held by a natural person, qualifying family trust, or qualifying LLC; last month's rent counts as part of the security deposit, but first month's rent does not.
D007.key_value: 1 month's rent; qualifying small-landlord exception up to 2 months' rent

coverage.small_owner_exception: Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total can charge up to two months' rent if ownership is held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC where all members are natural persons.
coverage.summary: Applies to many California rental units, with a higher cap for qualifying small landlords described by ownership and portfolio size.

D007.interaction: The page states that Assembly Bill 12 changed the amount landlords can charge statewide starting July 1, 2024, and separately notes Berkeley Rent Board cannot decide whether a particular landlord may charge one or two months' rent.

Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may only charge one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units
Starting July 1, 2024, landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total can charge up to two months' rent for furnished and unfurnished units if ownership is held by a natural person, family trust, or limited liability company (LLC) where all members are natural persons

D007.title: State security deposit deductions, inspection, documentation, and return rules
D007.requirement: Landlords must offer a walk-through inspection during the last two weeks of a tenancy, may deduct only reasonably necessary amounts for allowed purposes, and must return the remaining security deposit within 21 days after the tenant leaves the unit vacant with an itemized statement and required documentation if deductions are taken. The page also states added photo or proof requirements for certain dates: proof repairs were completed starting January 1, 2025; post-possession photographs starting April 1, 2025; and move-in photographs for tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025.
D007.key_value: 21 days; walk-through during last two weeks of tenancy

coverage.summary: Applies to California rental tenancies covered by the state security-deposit rules described on the page; no building age, unit-count, or owner-occupancy limit is stated.

D007.exemptions: Deductions are limited to rent default; tenant- or guest-caused damage beyond normal wear and tear; cleaning to return the unit to the same cleanliness level as at the start of the tenancy for tenancies beginning after January 1, 2003; and, if allowed by the lease, restoring or replacing personal property or furniture, excluding ordinary wear and tear.
D007.interaction: The page presents these as state-law security-deposit basics, while Berkeley's Rent Ordinance separately imposes security-deposit interest requirements for covered Berkeley units.
D007.quoted_span:
All or any remaining portion of a security deposit must be returned
within 21 days
after the tenant/s leave the unit vacant. If deductions were made, the landlord must give the tenant a written statement itemizing the amount of and and purpose for any security deposit deductions

D007.law_name: Berkeley Rent Ordinance security deposit interest requirements
D007.title: Security deposit interest for Berkeley Rent Ordinance units
D007.requirement: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before year-end.
D007.key_value: Annual security-deposit interest plus prorated move-out interest

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies only to units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance; the page does not define that coverage.
coverage.summary: Covers tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance.

D007.interaction: The page distinguishes this Berkeley Rent Ordinance interest rule from the state-law security-deposit basics described elsewhere on the page.
D007.quoted_span: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.

D008.requirement: Eligible Berkeley landlords may increase 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% for 2026, but not before January 1, 2026. D010.law_name: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
D010.title: Fair chance tenant screening rules for covered Boston housing providers
D010.requirement: Covered housing providers may not use a blanket policy denying housing because of arrests or convictions, and must assess criminal history case by case while excluding specified records such as non-conviction arrests, juvenile records, and convictions more than 5 years old except in limited safety-related circumstances. Agents also may not use an applicant’s credit score to approve or deny housing applications, and may use credit history only in limited circumstances when rental history is unavailable.
D010.key_value: No blanket criminal-history denial; convictions more than 5 years old generally excluded; credit score may not be used to approve or deny

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development funding and/or land, providers with income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy, and the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.
coverage.summary: The policy applies to certain publicly supported, inclusionary, or affirmative-marketing housing in Boston rather than to all rental housing citywide.

D010.exemptions: Tenant selection limits related to arrests and convictions do not apply where there is a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought or an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others; the guidance does not apply to current criminal behavior; and conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements preempt the policy.
D010.interaction: The document states that federal or state criminal-history requirements preempt this policy when they conflict, and that the policy is also applied to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.
D010.quoted_span:
Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or 
land, or that have income restricted units created under the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency (BPDA) Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions.

D012.requirement: In Boston, property owners may not discriminate when renting housing based on protected characteristics, including race, color, religion, disability, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity or expression, age, sexual orientation, marital status, rental assistance, family status, or military status.

D013.title: Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources when ending a tenancy
D013.requirement: Landlords planning to end a tenancy agreement must give the renter a Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources at the same time as the notice to quit or notice of non-renewal. Landlords and foreclosing owners must also submit tenant contact information and a copy of the notice to the City through the online portal.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when a landlord is planning to end a tenancy agreement; the City submission requirement also applies to foreclosing owners.
coverage.summary: All Boston landlords planning to end a tenancy agreement are covered.

D013.penalty: 1st offense: warning; 2nd and subsequent offenses: $300 per day. Failure to submit required information may result in a fine up to $300 per day.
D013.interaction: The document states that a landlord’s violation does not halt the eviction process.
D013.quoted_span: The Housing Stability Notification Act requires any landlord to provide renters with a Notice of Tenant’s Rights and Resources when planning to end a tenancy agreement.

D014.effective_date_basis: The HSNA becomes effective on November 6, 2020.
D014.title: Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources required when ending a tenancy
D014.requirement: When a Boston landlord serves a Notice to Quit or notice of lease non-renewal or expiration, the landlord must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources at the same time. Landlords and foreclosing owners must also send required notices and a certificate of compliance/service to Boston’s Office of Housing Stability.
D014.key_value: Notice required at the same time as Notice to Quit; 2nd and subsequent offenses: $300 per day

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when a landlord or foreclosing owner intends to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in the City of Boston.

to tenants when the landlord starts the eviction process, or when the landlord

D015.law_name: California Civil Rights Council Criminal History Housing Regulations
D015.title: Limits on criminal-history screening in rental housing
D015.requirement: Landlords may not use blanket bans against applicants with criminal records and may not consider arrests that did not result in convictions. Criminal-history screening must follow limits on what information is sought, how it is considered, and what action may be taken based on it.
D015.key_value: No blanket criminal-record bans; no arrests-without-convictions policies

coverage.summary: Applies to California rental applicants when a landlord uses criminal-history information in tenant screening.

D015.exemptions: The document states landlords are not entirely prohibited from checking an applicant’s criminal history, but must comply with the limits.
D015.interaction: The document says the California regulations built on HUD guidance identifying criminal-history screening as a potential disparate-impact fair housing issue.
D015.quoted_span: The California regulations include limits on what type of criminal history may be sought, how an applicant’s criminal history can be considered, and what actions a landlord may take based on an applicant’s criminal history. Blanket bans on applicants with a criminal record are prohibited, as are policies that consider arrests without convictions.

D015.law_name: SB 329 Source of Income Amendments to FEHA
D015.title: Ban on refusing Section 8 or other housing subsidies
D015.requirement: Landlords may not refuse to participate in government housing subsidy programs such as Section 8. A “No Section 8” policy is unlawful under the state fair housing source-of-income rules described in the document.
D015.key_value: Government housing subsidies count as source of income

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when an applicant or renter uses a government housing subsidy program such as Section 8.
coverage.summary: Applies to California rental housing decisions involving applicants or renters using government housing subsidies.

D015.penalty: The document states the California Civil Rights Department is cracking down on violators and filed a lawsuit against a landlord that refused to accept Section 8 vouchers.
D015.interaction: The document states SB 329 amended the Fair Employment and Housing Act definition of source of income to include government housing subsidy programs.
D015.quoted_span: In 2019, the California Legislature adopted SB 329, which updated the definition of “source of income” used in the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) to include government housing subsidy programs, such as Section 8.

D015.law_name: SB 267 Credit History Amendments to FEHA
D015.title: Credit-history alternative evidence for subsidized applicants
D015.requirement: A rental property owner may not use an applicant’s credit history in the application process when the applicant has a government rental subsidy such as Section 8 unless the owner offers the applicant the option to provide alternative evidence of a verifiable legal means to pay their share of rent.
D015.key_value: Alternative evidence required before using credit history for subsidized applicants

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when the applicant has a government rental subsidy such as Section 8.
coverage.summary: Applies to California rental applicants with a government rental subsidy when the owner uses credit history in screening.

D015.interaction: The document says SB 267 amended FEHA in addition to other recent state fair housing protections for renters using rental assistance programs.
D015.quoted_span: In addition, last year’s SB 267 amended FEHA to prohibit rental property owners from using a person’s credit history as part of the application process – if they have a government rental subsidy, such as Section 8 — without offering the applicant the option to provide alternative evidence of a verifiable legal means to pay their portion of the rent.

D016.title: California fair housing anti-discrimination and tenant-screening protections
D016.requirement: Housing providers and tenant screening companies may not screen, refuse, or treat applicants or tenants differently because of protected characteristics, including source of income such as Section 8 vouchers. A housing provider may consider criminal history only with limits: it may not use blanket bans, may not consider arrests without conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile matters, and any conviction-based denial must be directly related to tenancy or safety.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Owner occupancy, shared living area, senior housing, and homeless-youth housing exceptions depend on facts not stated in public assessor data.
coverage.summary: Applies to most California housing accommodations and most housing providers and housing-related service providers, including landlords, property managers, tenant screening companies, real estate agents, homeowners associations, mortgage lenders, and housing authorities.

D016.exemptions: When an owner occupies a home and rents to one additional person, the owner may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics but still cannot make discriminatory statements, notices, or advertisements. When sharing a living area in a single dwelling, the owner or occupant may state or imply that housing is available only to a person of one sex. Qualifying senior housing and, under some circumstances, housing for homeless youth may be limited based on age.
D016.penalty: Remedies listed include recovery of out-of-pocket losses, an injunction, access to housing denied, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, and attorney’s fees.
D016.interaction: The document states that complaints filed with HUD may be automatically filed with CRD, and complaints filed with CRD that allege facts violating the federal Fair Housing Act are automatically filed with HUD.
D016.quoted_span: Screening prospective tenants – including when done by a third-party such as a tenant screening company – in a way that discriminates based on a protected characteristic

D017.title: Residential rental application screening fee cap and refunds
D017.requirement: A landlord or agent may charge a residential rental applicant only for the actual out-of-pocket costs and reasonable time spent screening the applicant, capped at $30 per applicant as CPI-adjusted. The landlord must provide an itemized receipt, return unused amounts if no reference check or credit report is obtained, and provide any consumer credit report to the applicant within seven days of receiving it.
D017.key_value: Actual out-of-pocket costs and reasonable time, capped at $30 per applicant, adjusted annually by CPI beginning January 1, 1998

coverage.summary: Applies when a landlord or agent receives a request to rent residential rental property and charges an application screening fee.

D017.interaction: The section states it does not preempt federal or state housing-assistance program rules on deposits and fees and does not prevent a landlord from accepting a reusable screening report under Section 1950.1.
D017.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.

D017.title: Application screening process conditions when charging a screening fee
D017.requirement: A landlord or agent charging an application screening fee must either use a written-criteria, first-qualified-applicant process in the order completed applications are received and charge only when an application is actually considered, or return the entire fee to any applicant not selected. A landlord or agent may not charge a screening fee when they know or should know no rental unit is available or will be available within a reasonable time.
D017.key_value: First qualified applicant in order received, or refund entire fee to unselected applicants within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application submission, whichever occurs first

coverage.summary: Applies to landlords or agents charging residential rental application screening fees.

D017.exemptions: A landlord or agent who inadvertently collects a fee because of multiple concurrent application submissions does not violate the rule if the fee is refunded within seven days to an applicant whose application is not considered, or the applicant chooses to apply the fee to another rental unit offered by the landlord.
D017.interaction: The section states it does not preempt federal or state housing-assistance program rules on deposits and fees and does not prevent a landlord from accepting a reusable screening report under Section 1950.1.
D017.quoted_span:
Completed applications are considered, as provided for in the landlord’s established screening criteria, in the order in which the completed applications were received. The landlord’s screening criteria shall be provided to the applicant in writing together with the application form.
(ii)
The first applicant who meets the landlord’s established screening criteria is approved for tenancy.

D022.law_name: Cartwright Act Common Pricing Algorithm Provisions
D022.citation: Business and Professions Code Sections 16729 and 16756.1
D022.title: Ban on certain uses or distribution of common pricing algorithms
D022.requirement: A person may not use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of an agreement, trust, or conspiracy that restrains trade or commerce. A person also may not use or distribute a common pricing algorithm to coerce another person to adopt a recommended price or commercial term for similar products or services in California.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to any “person” using or distributing a “common pricing algorithm” as defined by the statute; the text is not limited to housing.
coverage.summary: The statute broadly covers persons using or distributing common pricing algorithms in California, without stating housing-specific building or tenancy coverage.

D022.exemptions: “Person” does not include the end consumer of a product or service.
D022.penalty: The Legislative Counsel’s Digest states that expanding the Cartwright Act expands activities whose violation is punishable as a crime, but the text does not state a specific penalty in this document.
D022.interaction: The statute states that nothing in this section impairs or limits the applicability of antitrust laws.
D022.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

D023.law_name: Civil Code § 1946.2 Just Cause Termination Protections
D023.effective_date_basis: This section shall become operative on April 1, 2024.
D023.title: Statewide just-cause eviction protections for residential tenancies
D023.requirement: After the tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential rental for 12 months, the owner may terminate only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause stated in the written notice; if additional adult tenants join, protection applies when all tenants have 12 months or one has 24 months. For no-fault terminations, the owner must provide relocation assistance or a final-month rent waiver equal to one month’s rent, and curable lease violations require a chance to cure first.
D023.key_value: Just cause after 12 months; if additional adult tenants join, all tenants 12 months or one tenant 24 months; no-fault relocation assistance or rent waiver = 1 month’s rent

coverage.small_owner_exception: Separately alienable residential real property, including a mobilehome, is exempt if the owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with at least one corporate member, or mobilehome-park management, and the required written exemption notice is provided to tenants.
coverage.other_unresolvable: Coverage depends on continuous lawful occupancy thresholds and exemptions based on use or status, including transient or tourist hotel occupancy, institutional housing, dormitories, shared bathroom or kitchen facilities with a resident owner, affordable-housing restrictions, and whether the person is a homeowner of a mobilehome.
coverage.summary: Applies statewide to residential real property after the tenant satisfies the 12/24-month occupancy thresholds, except enumerated categories including newer housing, specified owner-occupied properties, qualifying separately alienable homes, affordable or institutional housing, dormitories, transient housing, shared-facility housing, and mobilehome homeowners.

D023.exemptions: Does not apply to qualifying local just-cause ordinances as described in subdivision (i); transient and tourist hotel occupancy; housing accommodations in specified nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, licensed elder care, or adult residential facilities; dormitories owned and operated by schools or higher-education institutions; housing where the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains a principal residence there; single-family owner-occupied residences renting or leasing no more than two units or bedrooms, including an ADU or JADU, and mobilehomes; owner-occupied two-unit properties in one structure if neither unit is an ADU or JADU; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years unless it is a mobilehome; qualifying separately alienable residential property with required notice; specified affordable housing; and homeowners of mobilehomes.
D023.penalty: An owner’s failure to comply renders the written termination notice void. An owner who attempts to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, discretionary reasonable attorney’s fees and costs, up to three times actual damages for willful or oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious conduct, possible punitive damages, and injunctive relief sought by the Attorney General, city attorney, or county counsel.
D023.interaction: Residential real property is not subject to both this section and a local just-cause ordinance; qualifying pre-September 1, 2019 local ordinances and more protective later local ordinances apply instead, while less protective local ordinances adopted after September 1, 2019 are not enforceable unless this section is repealed.
D023.quoted_span: after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
D023.conflict_note: The section states it becomes operative on April 1, 2024, while the amendment note states: “Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 203, Sec. 1.   (AB 1529)   Effective January 1, 2026.”

D024.effective_date_basis: This section shall become operative on April 1, 2024.
D024.title: Statewide residential rent increase cap
D024.requirement: For covered residential rental property, an owner may not increase rent over any 12-month period by more than 5% plus the applicable cost-of-living change, or 10%, whichever is lower. If the same tenant remains in the unit, rent may not be increased in more than two increments during that 12-month period.
D024.key_value: 5% + CPI, max 10%; no more than two increases in 12 months for same tenant

coverage.small_owner_exception: Separately alienable residential real property, including a mobilehome, is exempt if the owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with at least one corporate member, or mobilehome park management, and the required written exemption notice is provided.
coverage.other_unresolvable: Exemptions also depend on deed or regulatory affordable-housing restrictions or subsidy agreements, school dormitory ownership and operation, stricter local rent or price control, ADU/JADU status in an owner-occupied two-unit property, and whether the occupant is a homeowner of a mobilehome.
coverage.summary: Applies statewide to residential rental units, including units in mobilehome parks, unless a listed exemption applies such as newer housing, certain affordable housing, school dormitories, stricter local rent-controlled units, qualifying separately alienable homes, owner-occupied duplexes, or mobilehome homeowners.

D024.exemptions: Does not apply to deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education or K-12 institutions; housing subject to valid local rent or price control that restricts annual increases to less than the state cap; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years unless the housing is a mobilehome; qualifying separately alienable residential property with required notice and non-corporate/non-REIT ownership; certain owner-occupied two-unit single-structure properties where neither unit is an ADU or JADU; or a homeowner of a mobilehome.
D024.penalty: An owner who demands, accepts, receives, or retains rent above the maximum is liable in a civil action for injunctive relief, excess-rent damages, discretionary reasonable attorney’s fees and costs, and, for willful or oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious conduct, up to treble damages; the Attorney General, city attorney, or county counsel may enforce and seek injunctive relief.
D024.interaction: The section excludes housing already subject to valid local rent or price control with lower annual increases and states that it does not expand or limit local authority to regulate rents consistently with Chapter 2.7 commencing with Section 1954.50.
D024.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower

D025.title: California residential security deposit limits and return rules
D025.requirement: For residential rentals, a landlord generally may not demand or receive a security deposit greater than one month’s rent, must use it only for authorized purposes such as unpaid rent, tenant-caused damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, and necessary cleaning, and must return the remainder with an itemized statement no later than 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Tenants may request an initial inspection before move-out, and bad-faith retention or claims against the deposit can expose the landlord to statutory damages.
D025.key_value: 1 month’s rent; qualifying small-landlord exception up to 2 months’ rent; return/accounting within 21 calendar days; bad-faith damages up to 2x security

coverage.small_owner_exception: A landlord who is a natural person, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, and who owns no more than two residential rental properties totaling no more than four rental units may demand up to two months’ rent as security, but this exception does not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member.
coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property used as the tenant’s dwelling.
coverage.summary: Covers security deposits and similar up-front security charges for California residential rental agreements.

D025.exemptions: The one-month cap does not prohibit an advance payment of at least six months’ rent if the lease term is six months or longer, does not preclude a mutual agreement for tenant-requested structural, decorative, furnishing, or similar alterations, and does not apply to security collected or demanded before July 1, 2024. Initial-inspection requirements do not apply when the tenancy is terminated under subdivision (2), (3), or (4) of Code of Civil Procedure § 1161. Certain documentation requirements do not apply if repair and cleaning deductions together do not exceed $125 or if the tenant validly waives them, subject to later tenant request rights.
D025.penalty: A landlord who in bad faith claims or retains security, or demands replacement security in violation of the section, may be liable for statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages; a landlord who in bad faith fails to comply with the 21-day return/itemization subdivision is not entitled to claim any amount of the security.
D025.interaction: The section excludes certain application-screening charges covered by Civil Code § 1950.6 and references Code of Civil Procedure § 1161 for some termination-related exceptions.
D025.quoted_span: (c) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), (3), or (5), a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

D026.title: Residential rental application screening fees
D026.requirement: A California landlord may charge a residential rental applicant only an application screening fee that does not exceed the landlord’s actual authorized screening costs and the statutory cap, adjusted annually for CPI. The landlord must not charge when no unit is available, must follow one of the statute’s fee/refund screening processes, provide an itemized receipt, return unused amounts, and provide any consumer credit report obtained to the applicant within seven days of receiving it.
D026.key_value: Actual out-of-pocket costs, capped at $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted annually beginning January 1, 1998

coverage.summary: Applies to landlords or their agents who charge applicants, including guarantors or cosigners, a fee to screen an application to rent or lease residential rental property in California.

D026.interaction: The statute states that it does not preempt federal or state housing-assistance rules on deposits and fees, and that nothing prevents a landlord from accepting a reusable screening report under Section 1950.1.

D027.title: Housing discrimination and rental screening restrictions
D027.requirement: Landlords may not discriminate in renting housing based on protected characteristics, including source of income such as public assistance and housing subsidies. For applicants with a government rent subsidy, a landlord must base financial eligibility on the tenant-paid portion of rent and, if using credit history, must offer and reasonably consider lawful alternative evidence of ability to pay.
D027.key_value: Income standard based on the portion of rent to be paid by the tenant

coverage.summary: Covers rental housing accommodations statewide, with specific screening protections for applicants or tenants using government rent subsidies.

D027.exemptions: The section states that it does not limit an owner’s ability to request information or documentation to verify employment, request landlord references, or verify identity; it also states that asking about the level or source of income is not discrimination based on source of income.

D028.title: Ban on collusive or coercive use of common pricing algorithms
D028.requirement: Businesses, including apartment rental companies, may not use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of an agreement to restrain trade. They also may not use or offer a common pricing algorithm to coerce users to adopt the algorithm’s pricing or commercial-term recommendations in California.

D029.title: Fair housing discrimination restrictions in Cambridge housing transactions
D029.requirement: Landlords, sellers, and rental agents in Cambridge may not discriminate in rental housing transactions or tenancy terms based on protected categories such as disability, race, national origin, family status, source of income, marital status, sex, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, age, religion, military status, relationship status, or family structure. Tenant selection standards must be reasonable and applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.

D032.requirement: For covered rental housing, rents are controlled at the base rent level, and rent increases are void unless authorized by Chapter 155. At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, the landlord may not request or receive more than the lesser of 5% or the applicable CPI percentage differential, and generally may impose no more than one cost-of-living increase in any twelve-month period.

D032.requirement: Landlords may not charge rent above the amount authorized by Chapter 155, and capital-improvement or hardship increases require Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board approval. The tenant can avoid termination in the possession action by paying or tendering all rent then due, with interest and court costs, on or before the day the answer is due.

D050.exemptions: If nonpayment was caused by failure or delay of the federal government, the commonwealth, a municipality, or their departments, agencies, or authorities in mailing or delivering a subsistence or rental payment, check, or voucher other than salary, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days and treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent due with interest and costs is tendered within that time.

D051.title: Notice to determine estate at will
D051.requirement: Either party may terminate an estate at will with written notice: generally three months, or if rent is payable more frequently than every three months, the payment interval or 30 days, whichever is longer. For nonpayment by a tenant at will, a landlord may terminate with 14 days’ written notice to quit, but a tenant who has not received a similar notice in the prior 12 months can prevent termination by paying all rent due within 10 days after receiving the notice.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to estates at will and tenants at will.

D052.effective_date_basis: as amended by 2025, 9, Secs. 54 and 55 effective August 1, 2025
D052.title: Massachusetts residential security deposit and move-in payment limits
D052.requirement: At or before the start of a tenancy, a landlord or the landlord’s agent may not require more than first month’s rent, last month’s rent, a security deposit equal to one month’s rent, and key/lock costs. A security deposit must be receipted, supported by a statement of condition, kept in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, and returned with allowable deductions within 30 days after the tenancy ends.
D052.key_value: Security deposit equal to first month’s rent; 5% or actual bank interest; return within 30 days; treble damages for specified violations

coverage.other_unresolvable: Does not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of 100 days or less in duration if for a vacation or recreational purpose.
coverage.summary: Applies to residential real property tenancies in Massachusetts, except short vacation or recreational tenancies of 100 days or less.

D052.exemptions: The section does not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of 100 days or less in duration when the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose.
D052.penalty: A landlord who fails to comply with specified security-deposit duties forfeits the right to retain any portion of the deposit; for failures covered by subsection (7), the tenant is awarded three times the deposit or balance owed, 5% interest from when payment became due, court costs, and reasonable attorney’s fees. Failure to pay required interest within 30 days after termination can result in treble damages for the unpaid interest plus costs and reasonable attorney’s fees.
D052.quoted_span: (iii) a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2);

D053.title: Reprisal for reporting violations or tenant union activity prohibited
D053.requirement: A landlord or agent may not threaten or take reprisals against a residential tenant for enforcing housing laws, reporting suspected housing-code or related violations, exercising specified utility rights, or organizing or joining a tenants’ union. A termination notice, rent increase, or substantial change in tenancy terms within six months after protected activity is presumed retaliatory, except a termination notice for nonpayment of rent.
D053.key_value: 6-month rebuttable presumption; damages of 1 to 3 months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when a residential tenant engaged in protected enforcement, reporting, utility-rights, or tenant-union activity.
coverage.summary: Covers tenants of residential premises in Massachusetts who engage in specified protected housing-related activity.

D053.exemptions: The statutory presumption for a notice of termination of tenancy excludes termination for nonpayment of rent.
D053.penalty: Landlord or agent is liable for damages of not less than one month's rent and not more than three months' rent, or actual damages sustained by the tenant, whichever is greater, plus costs of suit including a reasonable attorney's fee.
D053.interaction: The protected activity includes enforcing or reporting violations of federal, state, or local laws, regulations, by-laws, or ordinances regulating residential premises.
D053.quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action

D054.title: Landlord ban on rental application fees
D054.requirement: Massachusetts landlords/lessors may not require rental applicants or incoming tenants to pay application, pet, cleaning, amenity, credit-check, background-check, or other extra upfront fees. Before tenancy, a landlord may ask only for first month’s rent, last month’s rent, a security deposit, and a lock-change fee.
D054.key_value: Only first month’s rent, last month’s rent, security deposit, and lock-change fee may be required before tenancy

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to lessors before the beginning of a tenancy; the document does not state building-age, unit-count, or occupancy limits.
coverage.summary: Covers Massachusetts lessors/landlords charging prospective or incoming tenants before a tenancy begins.

D054.exemptions: The document says licensed brokers, unlike landlords, can charge application fees under broker rules; landlords may recoup screening costs through rent rather than a direct fee.
D054.penalty: The document reports that in Perry v Equity Residential Management, LLC, a federal district court awarded tenants treble damages and attorney’s fees over unlawful up-front application fees.
D054.interaction: The document contrasts this landlord fee ban with 254 C.M.R. 7, under which licensed brokers may charge fees if they comply with broker regulations.
D054.quoted_span: Massachusetts landlord tenant law spells out the list of charges that landlords may ask tenants to pay at the start of a tenancy: first month’s rent, last month’s rent, security deposit, and lock-change fee. M.G.L. c. 186, §15B. That is all. Landlords are not allowed to request additional charges.

D054.title: Licensed broker fees for prospective tenants
D054.requirement: A licensed broker may charge prospective tenants a fee, including an application-related fee, if the broker complies with broker regulations. The broker must give written notice of the fee amount, when and how it is paid, and whether it depends on a lease being signed, and the applicant must sign or the broker must record refusal.
D054.key_value: Written fee disclosure at first personal meeting

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to licensed brokers or salesmen finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee; landlord-brokers may face separate factual/legal issues.
coverage.summary: Covers Massachusetts licensed brokers dealing with prospective residential tenants for a fee.

D054.exemptions: Unlicensed persons may not engage in finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee. The document notes uncertainty for landlords who are also licensed brokers unless operating as a separate bona fide brokerage business.
D054.interaction: The document states brokers may charge fees where landlords generally may not under M.G.L. c. 186, §15B, but cautions that landlord-broker situations lack a definitive Massachusetts appellate ruling.
D054.quoted_span: In addition to holding a valid license, the broker has to tell the applicant in writing the amount of the broker’s fee, the time and manner of payment, and whether it is contingent on the owner and applicant actually entering into a lease or rental agreement.

D055.law_name: An Initiative Petition to Protect Tenants by Limiting Rent Increases
D055.title: Proposed statewide rent-control cap blocked from November 2026 ballot
D055.requirement: The blocked initiative would have capped annual rent increases for most Massachusetts residential rental units at the lesser of CPI or 5%. It would have exempted certain owner-occupied, newly constructed, publicly regulated, short-term, educational, religious, and nonprofit facilities.
D055.key_value: lesser of annual CPI increase or 5%

coverage.other_unresolvable: Exemptions for certain publicly regulated units, short-term rentals, and dwelling units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or nonprofit purposes.

D055.title: Massachusetts statutory ban on rent control
D055.requirement: Massachusetts law contains a statutory ban on rent control. Local rent-control limits are barred unless the state law is changed or repealed.

coverage.summary: Applies statewide as a ban on rent control.

D055.interaction: The blocked Initiative Petition 25-21 would have repealed this statutory ban and replaced it with a statewide annual rent-increase cap.
D055.quoted_span: The petition would have repealed the Commonwealth’s existing statutory ban on rent control, G.L. c. 40P, and replaced it with a statewide cap on annual rent increases for most residential rental units.

D056.title: CORI rules for housing applicant screening
D056.requirement: Landlords, property managers, real estate agents, and public housing authorities that use CORI to screen rental applicants must request it only as allowed, generally as the final step in the application process, and must follow consent, disclosure, storage, use, and dissemination limits. Before an adverse housing decision based on CORI or criminal history information, the applicant must receive required notices, a copy/source of the information, and an opportunity to dispute or appeal as applicable.
D056.key_value: CORI only as final step; retain CORI no longer than 7 years from last residency or housing decision, whichever is later

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to landlords, real estate agents, public housing authorities, and property management companies that request CORI to screen applicants for rental or lease of housing; provisions distinguish market-rate housing from subsidized housing.
coverage.summary: Covers Massachusetts housing providers and public housing authorities that request CORI for rental or lease applicant screening.

D056.exemptions: Nothing in the regulation prohibits a landlord, property management company, real estate agent, or public housing authority from making an adverse housing decision based on an applicant’s refusal to consent to a lawful CORI request; the regulation also does not limit access to CORI under other sections of 803 CMR 2.00 for other purposes.
D056.penalty: Improper access to, or dissemination of, national criminal history information may result in both criminal and civil sanctions.
D056.interaction: The regulation requires compliance with applicable federal and state laws, incorporates related CORI regulations, and imposes Fair Credit Reporting Act-related procedures when a consumer reporting agency is used.
D056.quoted_span:
803 CMR 5.00 sets forth requirements for the use of CORI for evaluating applicants for the
             rental or lease of housing, as well as for the storage and dissemination of CORI.

D058.law_name: Notice to quit for nonpayment of rent
D058.citation: General Law - Part II, Title I, Chapter 186, Section 31
D058.title: Notice to quit for nonpayment of rent
D058.requirement: A landlord giving a residential tenant a written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent must include the required state form with repayment-agreement documentation and information about rental assistance, court rules, and eviction restrictions. In a nonpayment eviction, the court may not accept the writ, summons, or complaint without proof that the landlord delivered the form.
D058.key_value: form required with notice to quit; information in 5 most common languages in addition to English

coverage.summary: Applies to written notices to quit for nonpayment of rent given by landlords to residential tenants, and to nonpayment summary process filings for residential dwelling units.

D058.quoted_span: A notice to quit for nonpayment of rent given in writing by a landlord to a residential tenant pursuant to this chapter shall be accompanied by a form that shall include, but not be limited to: (i) documentation of any agreements between the tenant and landlord for the tenant to repay the landlord for nonpayment of rent;

D059.title: Struck Massachusetts rent control ballot proposal
D059.requirement: The proposed ballot question would have limited annual rent increases for residences, but the Supreme Judicial Court ruled it could not go forward to voters. Renters cannot rely on it as an operative rent cap because it was struck before the November ballot.

coverage.other_unresolvable: The proposal carved out exemptions for several types of units, including units operated solely for religious purposes.
coverage.summary: The proposal would have applied to residences, with exemptions for several types of units.

D059.exemptions: The proposal included exemptions for several types of units, including units “operated solely for … religious … purposes.”
D059.interaction: The court held the petition could not appear on the ballot because its religious exemption meant it related to religion, which the state Constitution does not allow to go before voters.
D059.quoted_span: The proposal limits annual rent increases for residences, but it carved out exemptions for several types of units, including ones “operated solely for … religious … purposes." As a result, the court said it concluded the petition “relates to religion, religious practices or religious institutions,”

D060.law_name: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
D060.effective_date_basis: The FAIR Act takes effect on July 1, 2027
D060.title: Prohibition on algorithmic rent-setting practices
D060.requirement: Residential rental property owners may not use algorithmic revenue management software that uses competitors' nonpublic leasing information to set or recommend rents. Software providers and other coordinators also may not use such software to facilitate agreements or coordinate pricing among competing residential landlords.
D060.key_value: Prohibits algorithmic revenue management software using competitors' nonpublic leasing information

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies based on use of algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that uses nonpublic, competitively sensitive information from multiple residential rental property owners.
coverage.summary: Covers residential rental property owners, property managers, software providers, and other coordinators involved in algorithmic rent-setting for residential rental properties.

D060.exemptions: The act does not prohibit spreadsheets requiring human analysis, publicly available rent estimation tools, traditional real estate listing databases, or government-administered affordable housing programs.
D060.interaction: The document says the act preserves existing remedies under the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
D060.quoted_span: The FAIR Act prohibits residential rental property owners from using algorithmic revenue management software that collects or processes competitors' nonpublic leasing information to set or recommend rental prices.

D065.effective_date_basis: This act shall take effect on the first day of the seventh month next following the date of enactment
D065.title: Restrictions on criminal-record screening in rental housing
D065.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider most criminal history until after making a conditional offer, and even then may consider only specified convictions within stated lookback periods or specified serious offenses. Providers must disclose criminal-history screening before taking an application fee, give reasons and an appeal opportunity if withdrawing an offer, avoid discriminatory criminal-record advertisements, and may not require drug or alcohol tests or drug-abuse-treatment information.
D065.key_value: Conditional offer required before criminal-record inquiry; lookbacks include 6 years for first-degree indictable offenses, 4 years for second- or third-degree, and 1 year for fourth-degree

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to a dwelling unit offered for rent by a housing provider for residential purposes, other than a dwelling unit in an owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.
coverage.summary: Applies statewide to residential rental dwelling units, excluding units in owner-occupied premises with four or fewer dwelling units.

D065.exemptions: Before a conditional offer, a provider may consider whether the applicant has ever been convicted of drug-related criminal activity for manufacture or production of methamphetamine on federally assisted housing premises and whether the applicant is subject to a lifetime State sex-offender registration requirement. The definition of rental dwelling unit excludes owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.
D065.penalty: Violations are enforced through the Division on Civil Rights; penalties may be up to $1,000 for no prior violation within five years, up to $5,000 for one other violation within five years, and up to $10,000 for two or more other violations within seven years. The director may also order cease-and-desist, compliance reporting, possible remedial housing offer, return of application fee, and payment to the applicant up to $1,000.
D065.interaction: The act states that nothing in it bars or affects independent rights or actions, including rights under P.L.1945, c.169 (C.10:5-1 et seq.).
D065.quoted_span: A housing provider shall not make any oral or written inquiry regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

D066.law_name: Residential Rental Property Application Fee Limit
D066.effective_date_basis: This act shall take effect on the first day of the fourth month next following the date of enactment
D066.title: Residential rental property application fee not to exceed $50
D066.requirement: A landlord or agent may not charge more than $50 for an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes. The cap is adjusted annually based on positive CPI changes beginning the January 1 following enactment.
D066.key_value: $50, adjusted annually by CPI if CPI change is greater than zero

coverage.other_unresolvable: Does not apply to a licensee of the New Jersey Real Estate Commission unless the licensee is the landlord.
coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental application or similar fees for dwelling-purpose leases or subleases, except units in one-family or two-family dwellings and certain New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensees.

D066.exemptions: The fee cap does not apply to a dwelling unit located in a one-family or two-family dwelling that is offered for rent, or to a licensee of the New Jersey Real Estate Commission unless the licensee is the landlord of the residential rental property.
D066.penalty: Violations are subject to a penalty of up to $500 for a first offense, up to $750 for a second offense, and up to $1,000 for each subsequent offense; the wrongfully charged amount is remitted to the applicant or prospective tenant from the collected penalty.
D066.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.

D067.title: Good-cause requirement for nonrenewal of residential leases
D067.requirement: A landlord generally may not refuse to renew a residential tenant’s lease, whether written or oral, unless the landlord has good cause. This protection does not apply to owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, motels or hotels, or transient or seasonal units.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Motels or hotels, transient units, and seasonal units are excluded.
coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental properties except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, motels or hotels, and transient or seasonal units.

D067.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, motels or hotels, transient units, and seasonal units.
D067.quoted_span:
No landlord of residential rental properties except t hose in owner occupied two or three 
family dwellings, motels or hotels, transient, or seasonal units may fail to renew any lease, 
regardless of whether it is written or oral unless they have good cause not to renew the lease.

D067.title: Security deposit cap and handling requirements
D067.requirement: A landlord who collects a security deposit generally may not collect more than one and one-half months’ rent, and any later annual increase may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Security deposit money remains the tenant’s property and must be held in trust in a qualifying New Jersey account or investment, depending on the number of units.
D067.key_value: 1.5 months' rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit

coverage.other_unresolvable: A tenant in an owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling may make the Security Deposit Law applicable 30 days after sending a written request to the landlord.
coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rental properties, including mobile homes, but generally excludes owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings unless the tenant invokes the law by written request.

D067.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are excepted unless the tenant makes the law applicable by written request; the stated deposit-account requirements do not apply to security deposits for seasonal use or rental.
D067.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less. Any additional 
yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

D067.title: Security deposit cap, holding, interest, return, and penalties
D067.requirement: A landlord may require no more than one and one-half months’ rent as security, including prepaid funds such as last month’s rent, and must hold the deposit in trust with required interest notices. After tenancy termination, the landlord generally must return the deposit plus interest within 30 days, less lawful itemized deductions, with shorter return deadlines after certain displacements.
D067.key_value: 1.5 months' rent; return within 30 days; double amount wrongfully withheld

coverage.summary: Applies to residential security deposits, with stated special rules depending on whether the landlord receives deposits for ten or fewer units or ten or more units.

D067.exemptions: The document states that the security-deposit investment-account section does not apply to security deposits for seasonal use or rental as defined in N.J.S.A. 46:8-19(d).
D067.penalty: A tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld plus court costs and reasonable attorney’s fees; willful withholding of deposits involving State or federal assistance may carry a civil penalty of $500 to $2,000 per offense; unlawful use of security-deposit money may be a disorderly-persons offense with a fine of at least $200 or imprisonment for not more than 30 days, or both.
D067.quoted_span:
The landlord may only require one and one -half times the tenant’s monthly rent as security and 
the first month’s rent at the inception of the lease.

D067.title: Prohibition on discriminatory rental screening and refusals
D067.requirement: A landlord or rental agency may not refuse to rent or discriminate in rentals based on protected traits including race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, disability, nationality, or lawful source of income. A landlord may still refuse an applicant for stated nondiscriminatory reasons such as insufficient income, overcrowding, zoning-occupancy violations, or poor credit history.
D067.key_value: Protected classes include lawful source of income

coverage.other_unresolvable: Exceptions stated for rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex, and age-restricted housing as it pertains to familial status.
coverage.summary: Applies to landlord-tenant relationships except stated owner-occupied and other listed housing situations.

D067.exemptions: Two-family owner-occupied dwellings; rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home; residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex; and age-restricted housing as it pertains to familial status.
D067.penalty: Landlords who violate the LAD are subject to substantial fines and penalties, up to $10,000 for a first offense, and may be required to pay monetary damages and rent the unit to the complainant.

The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), 
N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(g) to -(h), prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires

D067.law_name: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act rent-increase notice rule
D067.title: Rent increases require lease termination, notice, and must not be unconscionable
D067.requirement: A landlord cannot raise rent during the middle of a lease term; the old lease must be terminated and the landlord must offer a new lease with the increased rent. Before evicting for nonpayment of an increased rent, the owner must serve a valid notice to quit and notice of rent increase, and the increase must not be unconscionable or violate municipal rent-control ordinances.
D067.key_value: No mid-lease increases; increase must not be unconscionable

coverage.summary: Applies to rent increases for tenants where the landlord seeks to terminate the current lease and continue the tenancy at a higher rent; the excerpt states no building-size cutoff.

D067.interaction: The document states that rent increases must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.
D067.quoted_span:
A landlord cannot raise the 
rent mid-lease term. The old lease must be terminated, and the new lease must have the increased 
rental payment.

D067.title: Thirty-year exemption from local rent control for newly constructed multiple dwellings
D067.requirement: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent-control ordinances for 30 years after construction is completed. A tenant should check with the local rent-control board or municipal clerk to learn whether a unit is covered by local rent control.

coverage.summary: Applies to newly constructed multiple dwellings during the 30 years after completion of construction.

D067.interaction: The law exempts covered newly constructed multiple dwellings from municipal rent-control ordinances for the stated 30-year period.
D067.quoted_span:
Under the Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law ( N.J.S.A. 2A:42 -84.5), newly 
constructed multiple dwellings shall be exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period 
of 30 years following completion of construction of the building.

D067.law_name: Condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple conversion rent-increase restriction
D067.title: No rent increase solely to cover conversion costs
D067.requirement: If a building is converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership of units, rents may not be increased to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. The document states that this does not bar rent increases for new services or amenities.
D067.key_value: No increases for costs resulting solely from conversion

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when a building is converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership of units.
