D067.interaction: The document states the prohibition applies to all tenants in the converted building regardless of protected-tenancy eligibility as senior citizens or disabled persons.
D067.quoted_span:
If a building is converted to a condominium or cooperative form of ownership, or to fee 
simple ownership of units, rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the 
conversion (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31).

D067.title: Good-cause eviction protections for New Jersey residential tenants
D067.requirement: A residential landlord generally may evict or refuse to renew only for statutory good cause and through the court eviction process. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, and some also require a prior Notice to Cease; notice periods vary by cause.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Does not apply to transient or seasonal hotel, motel, or guest-house occupants, except hotel and motel occupants with no alternate residence who reside there continually; does not apply to a unit held in trust for an immediate family member who is developmentally disabled and permanently occupies the unit.
coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rental properties, including single-family homes, mobile homes and mobile-home park land, apartment buildings and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes.

D067.exemptions: May not apply to two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; does not apply to transient or seasonal hotel, motel, or guest-house rentals; does not apply to certain units held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member.
D067.interaction: For eviction based on nonpayment of a rent increase, the increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control.
D067.quoted_span: A landlord must have good cause to evict a tenant (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53). There are several grounds for a good cause eviction.

D067.title: Unconscionable rent increases cannot support eviction
D067.requirement: A landlord may seek eviction for failure to pay a rent increase only if the tenant received notice and a Notice to Quit, and the increase is not unconscionable. A tenant who believes an increase is unconscionable may withhold the difference between the old rent and the new rent for a court to decide.
D067.key_value: rent increase must not be unconscionable

coverage.other_unresolvable: Same Anti-Eviction Act coverage limitations: transient or seasonal hotel, motel, or guest-house occupants are excluded, except continuous hotel or motel residents with no alternate residence; certain trust-held units for developmentally disabled immediate family members are excluded.
coverage.summary: Applies within the Anti-Eviction Act’s coverage of most New Jersey residential rental properties.

D067.exemptions: Same Anti-Eviction Act exceptions, including possible exclusion for two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units and transient or seasonal guest housing.
D067.interaction: The document states that the rent increase must also comply with municipal ordinances, including rent control.
D067.quoted_span: The rent increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control.

D067.title: Ban on self-help evictions and lockouts
D067.requirement: A landlord may not remove a tenant, lock a tenant out, shut off utilities to force a tenant out, or hold the tenant’s belongings without a court order or the tenant’s consent. Only a court officer may physically evict a tenant after a judge issues a warrant for removal.

coverage.summary: Applies to occupied rental premises and dwelling units in New Jersey as described in the document.

D067.penalty: A tenant who is illegally evicted may seek possession and damages; in a successful forcible-entry-and-detainer action, the court may award possession, all damages, court costs, and reasonable attorney fees. The landlord may also be charged with disorderly conduct if they refuse re-entry after police warning.
D067.interaction: This rule works with the eviction process by requiring a judgment and warrant before physical removal; it does not state any local preemption.
D067.quoted_span: Self-help evictions, or lockouts, made by the landlord are illegal in New Jersey.

D067.law_name: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act / Eviction Law
D067.title: Statutory grounds and notices for eviction
D067.requirement: A landlord may file for eviction only under specified statutory grounds, including certain conversion or owner-occupancy situations, termination of employment-based housing, or listed drug, assault, theft, human-trafficking, and related civil-liability grounds. Required Notices to Quit vary by ground, and misuse of certain owner-occupancy or removal-from-use notices can lead to treble damages and fees.
D067.key_value: Notice periods include 3 days, 2 months, and 3 years depending on the ground; up to five one-year stays in certain conversion cases; treble damages plus attorney fees/costs for specified violations

coverage.other_unresolvable: The excerpted grounds apply to specific situations such as condominium/cooperative/fee-simple conversion, employment-conditioned tenancies, and specified criminal or civil-liability conduct; broader Eviction Law coverage is not fully stated in this part.
coverage.summary: The excerpt covers residential eviction grounds and protections under New Jersey’s Eviction Law for specified conversion, employment, and misconduct situations.

D067.exemptions: No action may be brought against a senior citizen tenant or disabled tenant with protected tenancy status while that status or protected period remains in effect; several grounds also require that the lease expire before suit, and some offense-based grounds have two-year filing limits.
D067.penalty: If a tenant vacates after an owner-occupancy notice and the landlord does not occupy for at least six months, or if property removed from residential use is used residentially within five years, the landlord may be liable for three times damages plus attorney fees and costs; removal-from-use violations may also carry a civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation.
D067.interaction: The document also states that rooming and boarding houses, public housing, foreclosure situations, and protected-tenancy laws interact with or add to the Eviction Law’s protections.
D067.quoted_span: The landlord may file for eviction, if the owner of a building or mobile home park, which is constructed as or being converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, seeks to evict a tenant or sublessee whose initial tenancy began after the master deed

D067.law_name: Owner-Occupied Two- and Three-Family Dwelling Eviction Notice Rule
D067.title: Evictions from landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings
D067.requirement: Tenants in landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only by court order and only if the landlord proves one of the listed grounds, such as lease expiration, nonpayment, disorderly conduct, damage, repeated rule violations, or lease violations with a reserved right of re-entry. The landlord must give the applicable Notice to Quit except that no further notice is required before court action for nonpayment of rent.
D067.key_value: 3 months for at-will or year-to-year tenancy; 1 month for month-to-month and other tenancies; 3 days for disorderly, destructive, written-rule, or lease-violation grounds

coverage.small_owner_exception: Applies specifically when the landlord occupies a two- or three-family dwelling.
coverage.other_unresolvable: Whether the landlord occupies the property and the tenancy type determine the notice period.
coverage.summary: Applies to tenants living in landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings.

D067.exemptions: No further notice is required before bringing an eviction action when the tenant stays after failing to pay rent.
D067.interaction: This section provides special eviction grounds and notice periods for owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings apart from the general Eviction Law grounds summarized elsewhere in the document.
D067.quoted_span: Tenants of landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only when a court issues an order for eviction. However, in these cases, the landlord must prove that the tenant

D067.law_name: Regulations Governing Rooming and Boarding Houses
D067.title: Rooming and boarding house eviction good-cause and notice requirements
D067.requirement: Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the Eviction Law’s good-cause and notice requirements when evicting residents, unless the Bureau orders otherwise. The owner must also give the County Welfare Board at least three working days’ notice before starting an eviction action for any resident.
D067.key_value: At least 3 working days’ notice to the County Welfare Board

coverage.other_unresolvable: The building must have living units occupied by unrelated persons without private kitchens and bathrooms, unless an exception in the Rooming and Boarding House Act applies.
coverage.summary: Applies to rooming or boarding houses, generally buildings with at least two living units occupied by unrelated persons without private kitchens and bathrooms.

D067.exemptions: Exceptions include hotels with more than 85 percent temporary occupancy by people with homes elsewhere, school and college dormitories, buildings housing only college students, and certain residences for the disabled.
D067.interaction: The rule incorporates the New Jersey Eviction Law’s good-cause and notice requirements for rooming and boarding house residents, unless otherwise ordered by the Bureau.
D067.quoted_span: require owners of rooming and boarding houses to follow the good causes and notice requirements of the Eviction Law when evicting residents, except if otherwise ordered by the Bureau (N.J.A.C. 5:27-3.3(c)).

D067.title: Tenant protections after foreclosure
D067.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not a ground to evict a residential tenant in New Jersey. A new owner who bought a foreclosed property must give required notices, and a buyer who wants to personally occupy the home as a primary residence must give a 90-day Notice to Quit and may not evict before an existing lease expires.
D067.key_value: 90-day Notice to Quit for buyer personal occupancy after foreclosure; new owner notice within 10 business days after sale

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when a person acquires a foreclosed property containing residential rental units; notice method varies depending on whether the property has 10 or fewer dwelling units or more than 10 dwelling units.
coverage.summary: Applies to tenants in residential rental properties affected by foreclosure.

D067.exemptions: Month-to-month tenants and two- and three-family owner-occupied units are not exempt from the 90-day notice requirements.
D067.penalty: The document identifies prohibited pressure tactics in connection with monetary offers to vacate but does not state a specific penalty in this excerpt.
D067.interaction: The document states that federal foreclosure protections do not preempt any State or local law providing longer time periods or additional tenant protections.
D067.quoted_span: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. In Chase Manhattan Bank v. Josephson, 135 N.J. 209 (1994) the court held that when a lender or other buyer takes possession of the property, the residential tenant comes with the property.

D067.title: Protection against retaliatory eviction or nonrenewal
D067.requirement: A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by eviction, substantially changing lease terms, or refusing to renew because the tenant exercised protected rights. Protected conduct includes enforcing lease or legal rights, making good-faith health or safety complaints after notice to the landlord and time to cure, organizing or joining a tenant organization, or refusing retaliatory lease changes.

coverage.small_owner_exception: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are excluded from the reprisal law described in the document.
coverage.summary: Applies to all rental properties used for dwelling purposes, including mobile homes, except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings.

D067.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt.
D067.penalty: If a landlord takes reprisal action, the tenant may sue the landlord for damages in a civil action.
D067.interaction: This anti-reprisal protection operates alongside state and local tenant rights that tenants may attempt to enforce without retaliation.
D067.quoted_span: A landlord cannot take reprisal action against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of a lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when a tenant exercises certain civil rights (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10).

D067.law_name: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act
D067.title: Protected tenancy for seniors and disabled tenants in condominium or cooperative conversion
D067.requirement: Eligible senior citizens, permanently disabled tenants, and certain disabled veterans in a building being converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership may be protected from eviction for 40 years. To qualify, tenants must meet age, disability or veteran-disability criteria, have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date, and satisfy the stated income limit.
D067.key_value: Protected from eviction for 40 years; income not more than 3 times average county per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater; applications generally within 60 days

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to qualifying tenants in buildings being converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee simple ownership of units; eligibility depends on age, disability or veteran status, income, residence duration, and application process.
coverage.summary: Applies to qualifying senior, disabled, and certain disabled veteran tenants in buildings undergoing condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple conversion.

D067.exemptions: Protected status can end if the agency terminates it or the protected tenancy period expires; the document also states that applications generally must be filed within 60 days, although late filings may be accepted for good reason if conversion has not yet taken place.
D067.interaction: The document notes that tenants in Hudson County may be eligible for additional protected tenancy under the Tenant Protection Act of 1992.
D067.quoted_span: Tenants may be protected from eviction for 40 years if their family income is not more than three (3) times the average per person income in their county or $50,000.00, whichever  is greater (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.28).
D067.conflict_note: The document heading refers to the “Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act,” but one passage describes protected tenancy status pursuant to the “Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act of 1992,” while another cites the “Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act of 1981.”

D067.title: Additional protected tenancy in qualified counties
D067.requirement: The Tenant Protection Law of 1992 extends conversion-related protected-tenancy protections to qualified tenants in qualified counties who were not eligible as senior citizens or disabled persons under the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act. The document states that, at present, Hudson County is the only qualified county.
D067.key_value: Applies in qualified counties; document states the only qualified county is Hudson County

coverage.other_unresolvable: Coverage depends on being a qualified tenant in a qualified county and living in a building converted or being converted; the document states that the only qualified county at present is Hudson County.
coverage.summary: Applies to qualified tenants in qualified counties in buildings converted or being converted, currently described as Hudson County only.

D067.exemptions: Tenants who were eligible for protected tenancy as senior citizens or disabled persons under the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act are not the target of this extension.
D067.interaction: This law adds protected-tenancy coverage for certain conversion tenants who are not covered by the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act.
D067.quoted_span: The Tenant Protection Law of 1992 amendment extends protections to qualified tenants in qualified counties in buildings converted or being converted who were not eligible for Protected Tenancy as either Senior Citizens or Disabled Persons under the “Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act of 1981” (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.40 to -61.59; N.J.A.C. 5:24-3.1 to -3.4).

D068.title: Housing discrimination and lawful source-of-income protections
D068.requirement: A landlord may not discriminate in renting housing or in rental terms based on protected characteristics or a tenant’s lawful source of income, including Section 8 voucher income. Landlords also may not use discriminatory advertising, falsely deny availability, charge extra for a service or guide dog, or refuse reasonable disability-related modifications at the tenant’s expense.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Exceptions include renting a room in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling, religious-organization preferences for persons of the same religion, and the familial-status prohibition not applying to housing for older persons as defined in the LAD.
coverage.summary: Applies to the sale or rental of all property, including residential property, except certain owner-occupied small dwellings and specified religious-organization and housing-for-older-persons situations.

D068.exemptions: The document lists exceptions for rental of a single apartment or flat in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling; rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of an owner-occupied one-family dwelling; religious-organization preferences for persons of the same religion; and housing for older persons for the familial-status prohibition.
D068.quoted_span:
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses. This
means, for example, that a landlord cannot deny the

D069.law_name: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
D069.effective_date_basis: This act shall take effect on the first day of the twelfth month next following the date of enactment.
D069.title: Ban on algorithmic rent coordination for residential rentals
D069.requirement: Rental property owners may not pay for or use a coordinator, and coordinators or other persons may not perform coordinating functions or facilitate parallel pricing coordination for residential dwelling units. The ban targets algorithmic or automated use of competitively sensitive rental information to set or recommend rents, material lease terms, or occupancy levels.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to rental property owners and residential dwelling units intended to be used as a primary residence in New Jersey, with exclusions based on facility type.
coverage.summary: Covers New Jersey residential dwelling units used as a primary residence, including houses, apartments, and accessory units, and applies to owners of one or more such rental units.

D069.exemptions: “Algorithmic device” excludes certain non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis and databases that only query unprocessed data. “Coordinating function” excludes research, statistical analysis, or testing not used to set or recommend rental terms; public no-cost rent estimates; certain real estate brokerage databases; and government entities setting or limiting rents or sale prices through lawful affordability controls. “Residential dwelling unit” excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.
D069.penalty: A violation is unlawful and is a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act; the act states it does not limit application of C.56:9-6 through 9-17 to a violation of section 4.

D070.title: Annual rent increase cap for Newark rent-controlled dwellings
D070.requirement: For covered housing spaces, a landlord may not increase rent at lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy by more than the stated CPI formula, capped at 4%, and may not increase rent more than that in any consecutive twelve-month period regardless of vacancy, new tenant, or ownership change. The landlord must give the tenant and Rent Regulation Officer at least 30 days’ written notice, and no annual increase, tax surcharge, major new improvement surcharge, or hardship increase is allowed unless the dwelling is in substantial compliance and registration requirements are met.
D070.key_value: CPI increase from 15 months prior to 3 months prior, max 4%, in any consecutive 12-month period

coverage.other_unresolvable: Exemptions depend on use or program status, including public housing, transient hotel or motel space, commercial use, certain rehabilitated subsidized units, government-agency rent regulation contracts, and newly constructed or vacant dwellings as set forth elsewhere in the chapter.
coverage.summary: Applies to all multiple dwellings and housing spaces in Newark subject to the chapter, except listed exempt dwellings.

D070.exemptions: Exempt dwellings include public housing; motel or hotel space rented day-to-day to transients; commercial space; newly constructed multiple dwellings and vacant dwellings as set forth in Subsections 19:2-18.1 and 19:2-18.2; units rehabilitated by specified federal and state rental rehabilitation programs receiving Section 8 subsidies or federal vouchers during the subsidy/program tenure, with rents not exceeding HUD fair market rents; and rents regulated under a governmental-agency contract where that agency’s authority supersedes Newark’s authority during the contract period.
D070.penalty: A landlord must rebate rent collected above the chapter’s permissible amount by crediting the tenant over a period not to exceed 14 months, or refunding within one month if the tenant is no longer in occupancy; the rebate is retroactive to two years from the petition date.
D070.interaction: The chapter states that where a governmental-agency contract supersedes Newark’s authority to regulate the rent, the chapter is preempted during that contract period, but applies before the contract begins and immediately after it terminates.
D070.quoted_span:
At the expiration of a lease or at the termination of the lease
     of a periodic tenant, no landlord may request or receive an increase greater than the percentage increase in
     the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the CPI 15 months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase
     to the CPI three months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase.

D070.title: Newark rent control limits on excessive rents, hardship increases, utility surcharges, and rent decreases
D070.requirement: A landlord may not charge rent above the amount received on the chapter’s effective date unless the increase is authorized by the Newark rent control chapter. Hardship increases are limited to once in any 12-month period, utility surcharges require documented heating or water expense increases over 10% and are capped by building size, and tenants may petition for rent decreases when services are reduced.
D070.key_value: Unauthorized increases barred; hardship increases no more than once per 12 months; utility surcharge caps of 15%, 5%, or 3% of monthly rent roll depending on unit count

coverage.summary: The excerpt refers to rental units, dwellings, apartments, and tenants subject to the Newark rent control chapter, but does not state the chapter’s full coverage or exemptions.

D070.exemptions: No attorney's fees, accountant's fees or application fees incurred by a landlord in connection with an application to the Board may be included in determining whether the landlord is entitled to rent increases.
D070.penalty: The Rent Control Board may impose a monetary penalty not to exceed $500 for a violation of any provision of the chapter, after notice and an opportunity for hearing.
D070.interaction: The excerpt says rent above the chapter’s baseline is allowed only for increases authorized by the Newark rent control chapter, and hardship increases require substantial compliance with State and Newark codes.
D070.quoted_span: No landlord shall after the effective date of this chapter charge any rents in excess of what he/she was receiving from the effective date of this chapter except for increases authorized by this chapter.

D070.law_name: Newark Rent Control Regulations Retaliatory Eviction and Protected Tenancy Provisions
D070.title: Protection from retaliatory eviction and condo/co-op conversion eviction for eligible senior and disabled tenants
D070.requirement: A landlord may not bring an action to recover possession as retaliation for a tenant’s effort to secure or enforce rights under the Newark rent control chapter. The ordinance also provides an application process for senior citizen and disabled tenants seeking protected tenancy status from eviction due to condominium or cooperative conversion.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Protected tenancy for condominium or cooperative conversion depends on senior citizen or disabled tenant eligibility standards under the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.22.
coverage.summary: The retaliatory-eviction ban applies to dwelling units under the Newark rent control chapter; the protected-tenancy provision applies to eligible senior citizen or disabled tenants facing eviction from condominium or cooperative conversions.

D070.penalty: The Rent Control Board may impose a monetary penalty not to exceed $500 for a violation of any provision of the chapter, after notice and an opportunity for hearing.
D070.interaction: The protected-tenancy provision states that eligibility determinations are guided by the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.22.
D070.quoted_span: No landlord shall bring any action to recover possession of a dwelling unit as a reprisal for the tenant's efforts to secure or enforce any right under this chapter.

D070.effective_date_basis: This chapter shall continue in full force and effect from October 19, 1988.
D070.title: Newark rent control and annual increase limitations
D070.requirement: For covered Newark dwellings, rent is controlled at the applicable rent level and landlords may not institute rent increases except as allowed by the chapter. The Rent Control Board may not grant increases exceeding 25% in any one year for any tenant, and certain new construction, vacant-property, and rehabilitation exemptions or increases may apply.
D070.key_value: No increases except as provided; Board may not grant increases over 25% in any one year; substantially rehabilitated vacant apartment unit increase capped at 10% if spending equals at least 12 months of actual monthly rent

coverage.other_unresolvable: Newly constructed multiple dwellings may be exempt for the lesser of the initial mortgage amortization period or 30 years after completion; vacant dwellings may receive a five-year exemption if vacancy and rehabilitation-cost conditions are met; substantially reconstructed or rehabilitated dwellings may have unrestricted initial rent if Board determinations are made.
coverage.summary: Applies to dwellings to which Newark’s Rent Control chapter is applicable, subject to stated exemptions for new construction, qualifying vacant properties, and substantial rehabilitation.

D070.exemptions: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from periodic or regular base-rent increase limits for a period not exceeding the initial mortgage amortization period or 30 years after completion, whichever is less. Dwellings vacant for at least 18 months, or already vacant on the effective date of § 19:2-18.2, may be exempt for five years if rehabilitation or reconstruction costs during a twelve-month period exceed 50% of fair market value and code/CO requirements are met. Substantially reconstructed or rehabilitated dwellings may set unrestricted initial rent if the Board makes the required determinations.
D070.penalty: Violation of the chapter or misrepresentation before the Rent Control Board is punishable by a fine of not less than $100 and not more than $2,000, imprisonment for not more than 90 days, or both; the Municipal Court may also impose a monetary penalty not exceeding $2,000 for each violation.
D070.interaction: The chapter states that rent increases are barred except as provided in the Newark Rent Control chapter as amended and supplemented, and it incorporates state-law consequences for certain unlawful entries related to forced vacancy and rehabilitation.
D070.quoted_span: All rent for the rental of housing space and services in dwellings to which this chapter is applicable are hereby controlled at the rent level received by the landlord, as of the first date that this chapter was adopted, on September 4, 1985, and no rental increases shall hereafter be instituted, except as provided in this chapter as amended and supplemented.

D071.title: Unconscionable Rent Increase
D071.requirement: A residential rent increase may be treated as unconscionable if it is exceedingly harsh or unreasonable, exceeds the increase in the landlord’s expenses, and is not comparable to rents charged at similar properties. For properties with a redevelopment agreement or financial agreement, rent that exceeds the approved pro-forma is per se unconscionable.

D072.law_name: Newark Ban the Box Housing Ordinance
D072.title: Criminal-history screening restrictions for rental housing applicants
D072.requirement: For Newark rental housing, landlords and real estate brokers may inquire into or consider an applicant’s criminal history only after a formal application and must give written notice before conducting a criminal history inquiry. The ordinance limits what criminal records may be considered, requires consideration of rehabilitation and other factors, requires written adverse-action notice with results, keeps criminal-history information confidential, and bars ads referencing criminal-history screening.

D072.penalty: A first violation is subject to a fine of up to $500; each subsequent violation is subject to a fine of up to $1,000.
D072.interaction: The ordinance preserves federally or state-required or permitted criminal-history screening, but only for the offenses, offense types, and time periods that the federal or state law, regulation, or rule allows.

D073.citation: Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 7 of the San Diego Municipal Code
D073.effective_date_basis: Retitled to “Residential Tenant Protections” on 5-25-2023 by O-21647 N.S.; effective 6-24-2023.
D073.title: Just cause eviction protections and relocation assistance for San Diego tenants
D073.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a covered San Diego tenancy without at-fault or no-fault just cause listed in the ordinance. For no-fault terminations, the landlord must give required written notices and provide relocation assistance equal to two months of actual rent, or three months for a senior or disabled tenant, with additional re-rental and buyout protections in specified circumstances.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Excludes transient and tourist hotel occupancy, short-term residential occupancy, deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing except Section 8, mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law, specified institutional/care/nonprofit transitional housing, dormitories, shared-facility rentals with a resident landlord, certain owner-occupied single-family arrangements, and tenancies that do not continuously exceed 30 days or are fixed terms of three months or less including extensions or renewals.

D074.title: Ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices
D074.requirement: A person may not sell, license, or otherwise provide an algorithmic device to a landlord. A landlord may not use an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property in San Diego.

coverage.summary: Applies to landlords and persons providing algorithmic devices for residential rental property in the City of San Diego.

D074.penalty: A tenant may seek injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation against a landlord; each month and each residential rental property for which a landlord uses an algorithmic device is a separate violation; prevailing parties may recover costs and reasonable attorney’s fees; the City may also enforce through civil and criminal remedies.
D074.interaction: The remedies are cumulative and in addition to other remedies in the Division or at law, statute, or ordinance.
